transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a long story, but I suppose the main reason I'm sitting here today is because of the things I've been noticing lately. You see, I go down to the community center most afternoons to play dominoes with some of the other fellas. We've been doing it for years, just passing the time, you know? But recently, I've started picking up on things. The men at the table, they'll say certain phrases, use certain words... and I know, I just know, they're little messages meant specifically for me. It's not just them, either. Even when I'm at home, sitting in my chair with the radio on, listening to the news or the baseball game, the announcer will slip something in. A little warning. My wife, Mary, she gets so frustrated with me. She tells me, "Arthur, it's just talk, they're just talking about the weather or the game," but she doesn't hear it the way I do. She doesn't understand that they're warning me. They're telling me I need to be careful, that I need to watch my back. I try to explain it to her, I really do, but she just waves her hand and tells me I'm being foolish. But a man knows when he's being spoken to, doctor. A man knows.
Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?

Well, now that you ask about it... yes, I suppose I do. But it is not just some stranger making noise, doctor. It usually happens in the afternoons. Mary goes down for her nap around two oclock, and this old house of ours gets awful quiet. You know how a house settles when nobody is moving around. You hear the pipes clank a bit, or the wind brushing up against the siding. But then, right through all that quiet, I hear him. 

It is an old friend of mine. I will be sitting there in my chair, maybe just resting my eyes for a minute, and I will hear him call my name right from the front porch. Arthur, he says, just as clear as day. It is so clear, it is exactly like he is standing right there on the welcome mat, just waiting for me to come unlatch the screen door. And if he is not calling for me, he is humming. He used to be in the church choir years ago, and he had this real deep voice, and I will hear him humming a choir song out there. 

I will push myself up out of my chair, which takes some doing these days with my stiff knees, and I will shuffle over to the window to look out. I fully expect to see him leaning against the porch railing, but when I pull the curtain back, there is nobody out there. Not a soul. Just the empty porch and the street. I try to tell Mary when she wakes up. I tell her my friend was just out there humming, but she just shakes her head and tells me I was dreaming. But I was wide awake, doctor. You do not just imagine a choir tune coming through the wood of your own front door, plain as day.
Have you been drinking alcohol heavily lately?

Alcohol? Oh, no, no, doctor. I haven't been a drinking man for... oh, it's got to be decades now. I mean, sure, when I was a younger fella, back when I was working at the mill, the boys and I would sometimes head down to O'Malley's after a long shift. You know how it is when you're young and got a bit of change in your pocket and the dust from the day still in your throat. We'd have a beer, maybe two, just to unwind before heading home to the wives. But even then, I was never one to overdo it. My father, rest his soul, he had a bit of a heavy hand with the bottle, and I saw what that did to my mother, so I always kept a tight lid on it myself. 

And lately? Heavens, no. My stomach just wouldn't tolerate it these days anyway. Between the heartburn and the way my digestion acts up if I even look at something too spicy, I can't imagine pouring liquor down there. Mary wouldn't stand for it either. She runs a tight ship, my Mary. If she even smelled a drop of spirits on my breath, she'd have me sleeping on the davenport, stiff knees and all. So, no, doctor, no heavy drinking here. Just a cup of weak coffee in the morning and maybe some ginger ale in the afternoon if my stomach is feeling unsettled. That's about the strongest thing I put in my body.
Have you been having trouble with your memory lately?

Memory? Well... I suppose that depends on what you mean, doctor. If you mean, do I forget where I put my reading glasses? Sure, I do that. But who doesn't at my age? I'll set them down on the side table by my chair when I go to fetch the newspaper, and then I'll spend ten minutes looking for them in the kitchen. Mary always finds them right where I left them and gives me that look she has. You know the one. 

But my real memory? The important things? No, that's sharp as a tack. I can tell you the starting lineup for the '55 Dodgers, clear as a bell. I can tell you exactly what the weather was like the day Mary and I got married—it was unseasonably warm for October, and the leaves were just starting to turn that bright orange down by the creek. I remember the smell of the wood shavings at the mill like I was just there yesterday. 

Sometimes Mary will say, "Arthur, I told you to take the trash out," and I'll tell her she never said any such thing. But that's not me forgetting, doctor. That's just her thinking she said something out loud when she only thought it. She does that, you know. She gets busy with her knitting or her crossword puzzles and she thinks she's had a whole conversation with me, but she hasn't said a word. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm having trouble with my memory. My mind is perfectly fine, just... busy, I suppose. Busy with all those messages and warnings I told you about. You need a good memory to keep track of all that, don't you think?
Have you had any recent illness, head injury, stroke, or seizure?

A head injury? Or a stroke? Oh, goodness, no, doctor. The Good Lord has spared me from all that, thankfully. I mean, I have my everyday aches and pains, sure—like I mentioned about my stiff knees taking a while to get going—but nothing serious like a stroke or a seizure. I haven't even had so much as the sniffles this past winter! Mary is a real stickler about our health, you see. She marches us down to the corner pharmacy every October to get those flu shots, whether I want to or not, and she makes sure I wear a thick wool scarf if there’s even a hint of a breeze outside. 

As for hitting my head, well, I haven't had a bump on the noggin since... oh, it must have been the spring of '72. We had this terrible thunderstorm roll through, knocked a heavy oak branch right onto the gutters, and like a fool, I got up on the old aluminum ladder while the ground was still soft. The ladder slipped right out from under me in the mud. I came down hard and whacked my head on the stone birdbath. Mary came running out the screen door with a dish towel and a bag of frozen peas, hollering that I was going to be the death of her. 

But I haven't done anything foolish like that in a long, long time. When you get to be eighty-four, doctor, you learn to take things slow. You have to, really. You rush around, you trip on a throw rug, and the next thing you know you've broken a hip and you're lying in a hospital bed catching who-knows-what from the other patients. So I hold onto the banister when I take the stairs, I watch exactly where I step, and I just stay out of harm's way. So no, no recent illnesses or injuries or any of those terrible things you just mentioned. Just an old man trying to keep his footing, that's all.
Have you found yourself speaking in a way that other people say is hard to follow or doesn’t make sense?

Hard to follow? Making sense? Well, doctor, I wouldn't say that at all. Not at all. I mean, sure, sometimes Mary will give me that look—the one I told you about, where her eyebrows go all the way up to her hairline—and she'll say, "Arthur, what on earth are you going on about now?" But that's just Mary. She's got her mind on her knitting patterns or the price of ground chuck at the A&P, and she just isn't paying attention to the bigger picture. 

I speak perfectly clearly, if you ask me. I take my time, I lay out all the facts, just like I'm doing with you right now. You have to explain things properly, don't you think? If you just give a yes or no, people miss all the important details. Like the other day, I was down at the hardware store—the one on Elm Street, not the big new one out by the highway, I don't care for that one, it's too bright and the aisles are too wide, it doesn't smell like a hardware store should—anyway, I was talking to young Jimmy behind the counter about the right kind of nails for fixing a loose board on the back porch, and I was explaining to him how the wood swells in the humidity we've been having. I told him all about how the weather patterns have been changing, and how it ties into those messages I've been picking up on, the ones the government is sending through the television static. Jimmy just stared at me with his mouth half open, like a fish out of water, and then he said, "Mr. Higgins, I just need to know if you want galvanized or not." 

But that's not me being hard to follow, doctor. That's just young people today. They don't have the patience to listen to a full thought. They want everything in a hurry, zip-zip-zip, on those little phones they're always staring at. If they'd just slow down and listen to how all the pieces connect—the weather, the wood, the static, the warnings—they'd see it makes perfect sense. So no, I don't think I'm hard to understand. People just aren't trying hard enough to understand me.
Have you lost interest in seeing people or doing things you used to enjoy?

Lost interest? Well... I suppose it's not so much losing interest as it is... just not having the energy for it all anymore. I still love my family, doctor, don't get me wrong. Mary and the kids—well, they're not kids anymore, obviously, but they're still my world. But... things are just different lately. 

Used to be, I'd be out in the garden at the crack of dawn. I had the best tomatoes on the block, Big Boys and Early Girls, and I'd spend hours out there pulling weeds, tying up the vines, making sure the soil was just right. I used to enjoy that so much, feeling the dirt on my hands. And choir practice! Every Thursday evening down at the First Methodist, rain or shine, I was there. I've sung bass in that choir for forty-two years. 

But now... I don't know. Many days I just... I get up, I put my robe on, and I just sit at the kitchen table. Mary will pour me a cup of coffee, and I'll just sit there looking out the window at the bird feeder. The squirrels get into it, you know, they're terrible pests, but I don't even go out to chase them away anymore. I just sit there and say very little. Mary will ask me if I want to go to choir, or if I'm going to finally pull those dandelions that are taking over the front walk, and I just... I let it go by. I don't feel like moving. It's like my arms and legs are made of lead, and the thought of getting dressed and going out just feels like climbing a mountain. So I just stay at the table. It's quiet there, at least.
About how long have these messages and porch voices been happening?

How long? Well, now, let me think on that a minute, doctor. Time has a funny way of slipping by when you're not punching a time clock anymore, and the days sort of bleed into one another when you're just sitting around the house. But if I really sit down and trace it back... yes, it's been about nine months now. 

I remember specifically because it was right around the time Mary decided we absolutely had to have the living room carpets steam-cleaned. She hired this fellow from over in Shelbyville, and he came with this enormous, noisy truck and hoses running all through the front door. We had to sit out on the back porch for practically the whole afternoon while the rugs dried out, just staying out of the way. That was the very first time I really noticed the voices out there. Just murmuring, you know, right underneath the sound of Mary's wind chimes. 

And the messages on the television, those started right around the same time, maybe a few days later when we finally moved our chairs back into the living room and turned the set on. Now, it hasn't been every single day, mind you. It's not like a radio that's left on all the time. It's been happening on and off. Sometimes I'll go a week, maybe two, and the television static is just regular old static, and the porch is perfectly quiet except for the crickets and the neighborhood dogs. But then, sure enough, the patterns come back and the voices start up again, trying to tell me things. So yes, I'd say it's been going on just like that, on and off, for a solid nine months now. Mary thinks I'm just losing my hearing and getting confused by the neighbors' conversations, but I know what I'm picking up on. Nine months is a long time to be paying attention to something, doctor, you don't just imagine that.
Have you been seeing things that other people cannot see?

Seeing things? No, no, doctor, I wouldn't say that. My eyes aren't exactly what they used to be, mind you—I've got a touch of cataracts starting up in the left one, and sometimes if I stand up too fast I get those little silver floaters, like tiny minnows swimming across the ceiling. But as for seeing people or things that aren't really there? No, nothing like that. The Good Lord gave me enough trouble with my joints, I suppose He decided to spare my eyes for the most part. 

But... well, since we're talking about things that maybe other folks aren't picking up on... it's not so much the seeing, it's the hearing. I know I mentioned those murmurs on the porch earlier, but there's something else, too. 

Some afternoons, when the house gets completely quiet—you know, when Mary goes off to her sister's house to play cards and the television is switched off—the house just settles. It gets so still you can hear the refrigerator humming all the way from the front room. And on those quiet afternoons, I hear my old friend. 

It's the strangest thing, but it's as real as you sitting there in that chair. I'll hear him call my name, "Arthur," right from the back porch. Or sometimes he doesn't say my name at all, he'll just be out there humming a choir song. We sang together in the First Methodist choir for decades, you see, so I know his voice anywhere. He always had this rich, steady baritone, and I'll hear him humming "The Old Rugged Cross" or maybe "Rock of Ages." And it is so clear, doctor. I mean, clear like he is standing right there on the other side of the screen door, just waiting for me to bring him out a
Do you ever get confused about where you are or what day it is?

Confused about where I am? Oh, no, no. No, doctor, I know exactly where I am. I've lived in the same house on Elm Street for, oh, it must be fifty-two years now. Mary and I bought that place right after the youngest was born. It's a sturdy house, you know, built back when they actually cared about the framing. I know every creak in the floorboards, every draft from the windows. I couldn't get lost in my own home if I tried, not even in the pitch dark. 

And as for what day it is... well, now, that's a slightly different story, but not because I'm confused, mind you. Like I said before, when you're not punching a clock down at the plant every morning, the days do tend to blur together a bit. Monday feels an awful lot like Thursday when you're just sitting at the kitchen table looking out at the bird feeder. Mary keeps a big calendar on the refrigerator, one of those ones with the large print from the pharmacy, and she marks off the days with a big red X. So if I ever need to know, I just look at the fridge. But it's not like I wake up thinking it's 1985 or anything like that. I know it's the present day, I know who the president is—though sometimes I wish I didn't, if you catch my drift—and I know I'm sitting right here in this office with you. 

I suppose the only time I ever get a little turned around is... well, maybe when I'm listening to my friend humming out on the porch. Sometimes, just for a split second, it feels like we're back at choir practice, getting ready for the Easter service. But that's just a feeling, you know? A memory washing over me. I still know I'm in my own house. I still know it's whatever day Mary has marked on the calendar. My mind is sharp enough for that, doctor. I may not have had much schooling—I had to leave after eighth grade to help my father on the farm, you know how it was back then—but I've always had a good head on my shoulders for the practical things. I know exactly where I stand.
Is the old friend whose voice you hear someone who has died?

Well... yes. Yes, he is. That's... that's the thing of it, doctor. That's why Mary gets so upset when I mention I've been listening to him out on the porch. 

His name was Thomas. Thomas Miller. We knew each other for... oh, it had to be sixty years. We worked at the plant together, our wives were in the same garden club, and of course, all those years standing shoulder-to-shoulder in the choir loft. He was a good man, Thomas was. The kind of man who would give you the shirt off his back and then apologize that it wasn't ironed. 

He passed away... well, it's been about a year and five months now. It was sudden, you know. Heart just gave out on him while he was out pulling weeds in his tomato patch. One minute he was there, and the next he was gone. It was a terrible shock to all of us. Mary baked three casseroles that week just to keep her hands busy, and I... well, I just sat in my chair and stared at the wall for a good long while. 

And then, not too long after the funeral... maybe a few weeks, a month at most... that's when it started. That's when I first heard him humming on the porch. It's been going on ever since, for this whole year and five months. At first, I thought my mind was just playing tricks on me, you know, grief doing what grief does. I figured I was just missing him so much that my brain was filling in the silence with his voice. 

But it didn't stop. It just kept happening. And it's so clear, doctor. I know they say when people pass on, they go to Heaven and they're at peace, but sometimes I wonder if Thomas just... didn't quite make it all the way there. Or maybe he just misses the choir as much as I do. I haven't been back to church since he died, you see. It just doesn't feel right standing up there without him. So maybe he's coming to me, bringing the music to my back porch. Mary says I'm letting my imagination run away with me, that I need to let him rest in peace, but how can I do that when he's right there, humming "The Old Rugged Cross" as clear as day? It's been a year and five months, doctor, and he hasn't stopped visiting yet.
Has any doctor ever told you that you have dementia or Alzheimer’s disease?

Dementia? Alzheimer’s? Oh, heavens no, doctor. No, nobody has ever said anything like that to me. I see Dr. Higgins down at the family clinic—have been seeing him for, oh, it must be twenty-something years now, ever since old Dr. Miller retired and moved down to Florida. Anyway, Dr. Higgins gives me a full workup every single year right around my birthday in October. He checks the blood pressure, listens to the heart, taps the knees with that little rubber hammer... and he always makes a point to ask me those silly questions to test the memory, you know? 

He'll ask me to remember three words, like 'apple, table, penny,' or something like that, and then we talk about my cholesterol for ten minutes, and then he asks me to repeat them back. I always get them right, every time. I tell him, 'Doc, I might have had to leave school in the eighth grade to help my daddy run the farm, but there’s absolutely nothing wrong with my memory.' And he just laughs and says my mind is as sharp as a tack for a man my age. 

I mean, sure, I might forget where I set my reading glasses down from time to time. Just last Tuesday, I spent half the morning looking for them, turning the living room upside down, and wouldn't you know it, they were sitting right on top of the morning paper on the kitchen counter the whole time. Mary had a good chuckle about that, told me I'd lose my head if it wasn't attached to my neck. But who doesn't get a little forgetful about the small things at eighty-four? That’s just normal wear and tear, isn't it? It’s not a disease. 

Mary might call me stubborn as a mule, and she sure doesn't like me talking about hearing Thomas out on the porch, but she knows my mind is sound. She trusts me to balance the checkbook every month, and I never miss a penny. So no, no Alzheimer’s or dementia or anything of that sort. Just an old man with old joints and a perfectly good memory.
How old were you when these messages and voices first began?

How old was I? Well, let me think on that for a second, doctor. I’m eighty-four now, and like I mentioned, my birthday is in October. So if we count backwards... well, the voices and those special messages, they've been happening on and off for about nine months now. So I would have been eighty-three. Yes, eighty-three. 

Now, I know I told you earlier that I started hearing Thomas humming on the porch a month after he passed, which was over a year ago. But the humming was just... well, just music, you know? The actual voices, the ones that speak out, and those special messages I've been getting, that’s a more recent development. That started about nine months ago. I remember it clear as a bell because I was sitting in my favorite green armchair in the living room—the one with the worn-out fabric on the left armrest where I always rest my elbow. Mary has been threatening to throw that chair out or get it reupholstered for the better part of a decade, but I won't let her. A man gets used to his chair, you know? It molds to you over the years, and it fits me perfectly. 

Anyway, I was eighty-three, sitting right there in that chair, reading the afternoon paper, when the messages first started coming through. It wasn't just a hum anymore, it was real words, real messages. And like I said, it’s been on and off for nine months since then. Not every single day, mind you. Sometimes I'll go a few days or a week and it's quiet, just the birds outside at the feeder and Mary clattering around in the kitchen with her baking pans. But then, sure enough, they come back. It's funny how things change on you when you least expect it. You live in a house for fifty-two years, sit in the same chair, read the same paper, and then one afternoon when you're eighty-three, everything is just a little bit different.
Have you been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease?

Parkinson’s? No, doctor, no. Nobody has ever mentioned Parkinson’s to me. My hands are just as steady as they ever were. Well, I mean, I get a little stiffness in the knuckles first thing in the morning, especially when the weather turns cold and damp like it does around late November, but that’s just the arthritis talking. Dr. Higgins told me years ago that arthritis is just the price we pay for living a long life and working hard with our hands. And I did work hard, doctor. Forty years at the plant, plus all that time on my daddy's farm before that, hauling hay and fixing tractors. You use your hands that much, they're bound to ache a bit when you get to be eighty-four. 

But they don't shake. Not like that Parkinson’s. I knew a fellow once, old Charlie Henderson, who used to run the hardware store downtown before those big box stores moved in and pushed him out. Charlie got the Parkinson’s real bad in his later years. It was a crying shame to see, really. He’d try to count out your change at the register and his poor hands would tremble so much the nickels and dimes would just clatter right onto the counter. He had to have his daughter come in and run the till for him eventually, and you could tell it just broke his pride in two. 

But me? No, nothing like that. I can still pour a cup of black coffee right to the brim without spilling a single drop, and just last week I helped Mary thread a needle because her eyes get tired in the evening when she's trying to mend my socks. My eyes aren't perfect, mind you—I need those reading glasses I told you I keep losing—but my hands do exactly what I tell them to do. So no, no Parkinson’s disease. Just the regular old creaks and groans of an old machine, that's all.
Have you been seeing things that other people cannot see?

Seeing things? Oh, no, no. My eyes aren't what they used to be, like I was saying about losing my reading glasses, but I don't see anything that isn't there. No ghosts or shadows walking around the living room, nothing silly like that. But... well, hearing things, now, that’s a bit different. 

I know I brought up Thomas earlier, my old friend who passed away last year. Mary just hates it when I talk about this, she really does. She’ll just shake her head, purse her lips, and tell me to turn the television up louder so I don't get distracted. But I’m telling you the honest truth, doctor. Some afternoons, especially when the house gets real quiet—you know, around two or three o'clock when the mail's already been delivered and Mary is sitting at the kitchen table working on her crossword puzzles—I'll be resting in my green chair, and I'll hear him. 

I hear Thomas out on the front porch. It’s not just the wind playing tricks, either. I’ll hear him call my name, just as clear as a bell, or he’ll be humming a choir song. We used to sing together down at the church, both of us in the bass section, standing right next to each other for near on thirty years. So I know his voice, doctor. I know the exact way he hums those old hymns. And when I hear it out there on the porch, it is so clear, it's exactly like he is standing right there on the wood planks, just waiting for me to come out and offer him a glass of iced tea. 

I'll even look out the front window sometimes, half expecting to see him leaning against the railing in his brown suspenders, but... well, there's nobody there to see. Just the empty porch and the hanging ferns. So no, I don't see anything unusual, not a single thing. But I sure do hear him.
Have you been diagnosed with any major medical illness, such as a brain disease or another serious health condition?

Major medical illness? Brain disease? Oh, no, no, doctor. Goodness, no. Nothing like that. Like I said, I've got the arthritis in my hands, and my knees aren't quite as spry as they were back when I was climbing up on the tractors, but that's just normal wear and tear. You run a machine for eighty-four years, it's going to rattle a bit, isn't it? 

But my brain? No, my brain is just fine. I remember things clear as day. I can still tell you the exact day Mary and I got married—June 14th, 1958, a beautiful sunny Saturday, not a cloud in the sky. And I can tell you the names of all the fellows I worked with at the plant on the line. No, nobody has ever told me I have a brain disease or a tumor or... or whatever else might be serious like that. 

I mean, I go to see Dr. Higgins—well, it's Dr. Higgins' son now, young Dr. Higgins, since the older one retired and moved down to Florida. Young Dr. Higgins checks my blood pressure every six months. He puts that cuff on my arm, pumps it up real tight, and he always tells me, "Mr. Miller, your pressure is better than half the men my age." And I take a little pill for my cholesterol, just a tiny white one, because Mary insists on making her Sunday roast with all the trimmings, and you can't just eat plain chicken breast for the rest of your life, can you? But that's it. A cholesterol pill and some stiffness in the joints. No brain diseases, no serious health conditions. Just an old man who hears his friend singing on the porch sometimes.
During the times these messages and voices have been happening, have you also been feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say that. Not most of the day, and certainly not every day. I mean, sure, I have my moments, doctor. Who doesn't at my age? You sit around in the green chair long enough, watching the cars go by, and sometimes you get to thinking about the old days. You think about the folks who aren't around anymore, like Thomas, or my brother Henry who passed back in '98. Sometimes a little blue feeling washes over you, just a quiet sort of sadness, you know? Like when the sun goes behind a cloud for a few minutes in the late afternoon and the living room gets all dim and chilly. 

But it doesn't stay that way. It's not this heavy, dark thing that sits on my chest all day long. Mary wouldn't stand for it if it was! She’s always bustling about, keeping the house going. If she sees me staring out the window too long, she’ll come over with a cup of tea or ask me to help her sort the coupons from the Sunday paper. And I still enjoy things, doctor. I still like my morning coffee, I still like watching the game shows at seven o'clock—even if the questions aren't nearly as hard as they used to be when Bob Barker was on television. 

So, no, not depressed. Not really. When I hear Thomas humming out there on the porch, it doesn't make me feel sad or down in the dumps. Honestly, sometimes it’s almost... comforting, in a strange way. It just reminds me of the choir days. I might feel a little wistful, sure, but I’m not sitting here crying or feeling hopeless from morning till night. I just get on with things. That's what you do when you're eighty-four, you just keep putting one foot in front of the other.
Have you had a period of several days when you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep than usual?

Energetic? Less sleep? Well, now, that is an interesting question, doctor. Because Mary was just fussing at me about this very thing not two weeks ago. Usually, you see, we have our routine. We watch the Wheel of Fortune, maybe catch the ten o'clock local news, and then it's off to bed. At my age, you usually cherish a good night's sleep in a warm bed, especially with the arthritis and all. 

But every now and then... I don't know what gets into me, but I'll have these spells. They might last three or four days, sometimes near on a whole week, where my body just decides it doesn't need the pillow at all. On those nights I may sleep only two or three hours, then get up before daylight feeling ready to work like I had a full rest. 

It is the strangest thing, doctor. I'll lay my head down at ten, and by one or maybe half-past one in the morning, my eyes will just pop wide open. Wide open! And I'm not tossing and turning or feeling groggy, either. I'll feel so full of vinegar I can't just lay there staring at the ceiling, so I have to get up and do something. I'll go down to the kitchen, being real quiet on the stairs so I don't wake Mary, and I'll start finding chores. 

Last time it happened, I took apart the toaster to clean out all the burnt crumbs from the bottom, and then I got out my tools and oiled every single hinge on the kitchen cabinets. Mary came down at six in the morning in her pink robe, turned on the light, and just stared at me sitting there on the floor with a screwdriver. She said, "What on God's green earth are you doing up?" But I tried to tell her, I just didn't need the sleep! I felt fantastic. Back when I was working on the line at the plant, I would have paid good money to feel that spry for a morning shift. I could have worked a double shift and still had energy to mow the lawn. So yes, I do get those days where I just don't need much shut-eye at all and feel completely raring to go.
During those spells when you only slept a few hours, did you feel unusually cheerful or on top of the world?

Cheerful? Oh, doctor, cheerful hardly does it justice. I feel... well, I wake up feeling just incredibly bright, you know? Like the sun is shining just for me and I'm the man of the hour. I'll feel so important, like I've got all the answers to everything. During those weeks—and it can go on for weeks sometimes, mind you
During those spells, did you feel you had special powers or abilities that other people did not have?

Well, powers... I don't know if I'd call it magic powers, like you read about in comic books or see in those superhero movies the grandkids watch. Well... yes. Yes, he is. That's... that's the thing of it, doctor. That's why Mary gets so upset when I mention I've been listening to him out on the porch. 

His name was Thomas. Thomas Miller. We knew each other for... oh, it had to be sixty years. We worked at the plant together, our wives were in the same garden club, and of course, all those years standing shoulder-to-shoulder in the choir loft. He was a good man, Thomas was. The kind of man who would give you the shirt off his back and then apologize that it wasn't ironed. 

He passed away... well, it's been about a year and five months now. It was sudden, you know. Heart just gave out on him while he was out pulling weeds in his tomato patch. One minute he was there, and the next he was gone. It was a terrible shock to all of us. Mary baked three casseroles that week just to keep her hands busy, and I... well, I just sat in my chair and stared at the wall for a good long while. 

And then, not too long after the funeral... maybe a few weeks, a month at most... that's when it started. That's when I first heard him humming on the porch. It's been going on ever since, for this whole year and five months. At first, I thought my mind was just playing tricks on me, you know, grief doing what grief does. I figured I was just missing him so much that my brain was filling in the silence with his voice. 

But it didn't stop. It just kept happening. And it's so clear, doctor. I know they say when people pass on, they go to Heaven and they're at peace, but sometimes I wonder if Thomas just... didn't quite make it all the way there. Or maybe he just misses the choir as much as I do. I haven't been back to church since he died, you see. It just doesn't feel right standing up there without him. So maybe he's coming to me, bringing the music to my back porch. Mary says I'm letting my imagination run away with me, that I need to let him rest in peace, but how can I do that when he's right there, humming "The Old Rugged Cross" as clear as day? It's been a year and five months, doctor, and he hasn't stopped visiting yet.

inference.note: This turn clarifies the voice is of a deceased friend and began after bereavement, but the persistent delusions of reference/broadcast messages and months-long course still keep delusional disorder highest; psychotic disorder due to another medical condition remains possible given late-life onset, and schizophrenia remains less likely due to preserved organization and late onset.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is an identifiable organic brain condition underlying the psychosis by assessing for established dementia, which would favor F06.2 over primary psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Has any doctor ever told you that you have dementia or Alzheimer’s disease?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have ever been diagnosed with dementia or Alzheimer's disease. My symptom profile does not contain any information about a diagnosis of dementia or Alzheimer's disease.

patient.answer:
Dementia? Alzheimer’s? Oh, heavens no, doctor. No, nobody has ever said anything like that to me. I see Dr. Higgins down at the family clinic—have been seeing him for, oh, it must be twenty-something years now, ever since old Dr. Miller retired and moved down to Florida. Anyway, Dr. Higgins gives me a full workup every single year right around my birthday in October. He checks the blood pressure, listens to the heart, taps the knees with that little rubber hammer... and he always makes a point to ask me those silly questions to test the memory, you know? 

He'll ask me to remember three words, like 'apple, table, penny,' or something like that, and then we talk about my cholesterol for ten minutes, and then he asks me to repeat them back. I always get them right, every time. I tell him, 'Doc, I might have had to leave school in the eighth grade to help my daddy run the farm, but there’s absolutely nothing wrong with my memory.' And he just laughs and says my mind is as sharp as a tack for a man my age. 

I mean, sure, I might forget where I set my reading glasses down from time to time. Just last Tuesday, I spent half the morning looking for them, turning the living room upside down, and wouldn't you know it, they were sitting right on top of the morning paper on the kitchen counter the whole time. Mary had a good chuckle about that, told me I'd lose my head if it wasn't attached to my neck. But who doesn't get a little forgetful about the small things at eighty-four? That’s just normal wear and tear, isn't it? It’s not a disease. 

Mary might call me stubborn as a mule, and she sure doesn't like me talking about hearing Thomas out on the porch, but she knows my mind is sound. She trusts me to balance the checkbook every month, and I never miss a penny. So no, no Alzheimer’s or dementia or anything of that sort. Just an old man with old joints and a perfectly good memory.

doctor.intent: Determine the age at onset of the psychotic symptoms to distinguish late-onset primary schizophrenia from delusional disorder and psychosis due to a medical condition.
doctor.question: How old were you when these messages and voices first began?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and special messages have been happening on and off for about 9 months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking when the psychotic symptoms (messages and voices) first began. This matches the duration of psychotic symptoms, which indicates they started about 9 months ago.

patient.answer:
How old was I? Well, let me think on that for a second, doctor. I’m eighty-four now, and like I mentioned, my birthday is in October. So if we count backwards... well, the voices and those special messages, they've been happening on and off for about nine months now. So I would have been eighty-three. Yes, eighty-three. 

Now, I know I told you earlier that I started hearing Thomas humming on the porch a month after he passed, which was over a year ago. But the humming was just... well, just music, you know? The actual voices, the ones that speak out, and those special messages I've been getting, that’s a more recent development. That started about nine months ago. I remember it clear as a bell because I was sitting in my favorite green armchair in the living room—the one with the worn-out fabric on the left armrest where I always rest my elbow. Mary has been threatening to throw that chair out or get it reupholstered for the better part of a decade, but I won't let her. A man gets used to his chair, you know? It molds to you over the years, and it fits me perfectly. 

Anyway, I was eighty-three, sitting right there in that chair, reading the afternoon paper, when the messages first started coming through. It wasn't just a hum anymore, it was real words, real messages. And like I said, it’s been on and off for nine months since then. Not every single day, mind you. Sometimes I'll go a few days or a week and it's quiet, just the birds outside at the feeder and Mary clattering around in the kitchen with her baking pans. But then, sure enough, they come back. It's funny how things change on you when you least expect it. You live in a house for fifty-two years, sit in the same chair, read the same paper, and then one afternoon when you're eighty-three, everything is just a little bit different.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is an underlying medical or neurological condition causing the psychosis, which would support organic delusional disorder (F06.2) over primary psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Have you been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Parkinson’s? No, doctor, no. Nobody has ever mentioned Parkinson’s to me. My hands are just as steady as they ever were. Well, I mean, I get a little stiffness in the knuckles first thing in the morning, especially when the weather turns cold and damp like it does around late November, but that’s just the arthritis talking. Dr. Higgins told me years ago that arthritis is just the price we pay for living a long life and working hard with our hands. And I did work hard, doctor. Forty years at the plant, plus all that time on my daddy's farm before that, hauling hay and fixing tractors. You use your hands that much, they're bound to ache a bit when you get to be eighty-four. 

But they don't shake. Not like that Parkinson’s. I knew a fellow once, old Charlie Henderson, who used to run the hardware store downtown before those big box stores moved in and pushed him out. Charlie got the Parkinson’s real bad in his later years. It was a crying shame to see, really. He’d try to count out your change at the register and his poor hands would tremble so much the nickels and dimes would just clatter right onto the counter. He had to have his daughter come in and run the till for him eventually, and you could tell it just broke his pride in two. 

But me? No, nothing like that. I can still pour a cup of black coffee right to the brim without spilling a single drop, and just last week I helped Mary thread a needle because her eyes get tired in the evening when she's trying to mend my socks. My eyes aren't perfect, mind you—I need those reading glasses I told you I keep losing—but my hands do exactly what I tell them to do. So no, no Parkinson’s disease. Just the regular old creaks and groans of an old machine, that's all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is an underlying medical cause for the late-onset psychosis by checking for visual hallucinations, which would favor an organic psychotic disorder over delusional disorder or paranoid schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Have you been seeing things that other people cannot see?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Some afternoons, when the house is quiet, I hear my old friend call my name from the porch or hum a choir song, clear like he is standing right there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about visual hallucinations (seeing things that others cannot see), which falls under the Hallucinations symptom.

patient.answer:
Seeing things? Oh, no, no. My eyes aren't what they used to be, like I was saying about losing my reading glasses, but I don't see anything that isn't there. No ghosts or shadows walking around the living room, nothing silly like that. But... well, hearing things, now, that’s a bit different. 

I know I brought up Thomas earlier, my old friend who passed away last year. Mary just hates it when I talk about this, she really does. She’ll just shake her head, purse her lips, and tell me to turn the television up louder so I don't get distracted. But I’m telling you the honest truth, doctor. Some afternoons, especially when the house gets real quiet—you know, around two or three o'clock when the mail's already been delivered and Mary is sitting at the kitchen table working on her crossword puzzles—I'll be resting in my green chair, and I'll hear him. 

I hear Thomas out on the front porch. It’s not just the wind playing tricks, either. I’ll hear him call my name, just as clear as a bell, or he’ll be humming a choir song. We used to sing together down at the church, both of us in the bass section, standing right next to each other for near on thirty years. So I know his voice, doctor. I know the exact way he hums those old hymns. And when I hear it out there on the porch, it is so clear, it's exactly like he is standing right there on the wood planks, just waiting for me to come out and offer him a glass of iced tea. 

I'll even look out the front window sometimes, half expecting to see him leaning against the railing in his brown suspenders, but... well, there's nobody there to see. Just the empty porch and the hanging ferns. So no, I don't see anything unusual, not a single thing. But I sure do hear him.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is an underlying medical or neurological condition causing the psychotic symptoms, which best distinguishes organic delusional disorder from primary psychotic disorders at this stage.
doctor.question: Have you been diagnosed with any major medical illness, such as a brain disease or another serious health condition?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about other major medical illnesses or brain diseases, which is not covered by any specific symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Major medical illness? Brain disease? Oh, no, no, doctor. Goodness, no. Nothing like that. Like I said, I've got the arthritis in my hands, and my knees aren't quite as spry as they were back when I was climbing up on the tractors, but that's just normal wear and tear. You run a machine for eighty-four years, it's going to rattle a bit, isn't it? 

But my brain? No, my brain is just fine. I remember things clear as day. I can still tell you the exact day Mary and I got married—June 14th, 1958, a beautiful sunny Saturday, not a cloud in the sky. And I can tell you the names of all the fellows I worked with at the plant on the line. No, nobody has ever told me I have a brain disease or a tumor or... or whatever else might be serious like that. 

I mean, I go to see Dr. Higgins—well, it's Dr. Higgins' son now, young Dr. Higgins, since the older one retired and moved down to Florida. Young Dr. Higgins checks my blood pressure every six months. He puts that cuff on my arm, pumps it up real tight, and he always tells me, "Mr. Miller, your pressure is better than half the men my age." And I take a little pill for my cholesterol, just a tiny white one, because Mary insists on making her Sunday roast with all the trimmings, and you can't just eat plain chicken breast for the rest of your life, can you? But that's it. A cholesterol pill and some stiffness in the joints. No brain diseases, no serious health conditions. Just an old man who hears his friend singing on the porch sometimes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms are occurring in the context of a mood episode, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from an acute/transient psychotic disorder or an organic delusional disorder.
doctor.question: During the times these messages and voices have been happening, have you also been feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a major depressive episode (feeling depressed most of the day), which is not included in the patient's symptom profile (the patient has Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type, with manic symptoms but no depressive symptoms listed).

patient.answer:
Depressed? Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say that. Not most of the day, and certainly not every day. I mean, sure, I have my moments, doctor. Who doesn't at my age? You sit around in the green chair long enough, watching the cars go by, and sometimes you get to thinking about the old days. You think about the folks who aren't around anymore, like Thomas, or my brother Henry who passed back in '98. Sometimes a little blue feeling washes over you, just a quiet sort of sadness, you know? Like when the sun goes behind a cloud for a few minutes in the late afternoon and the living room gets all dim and chilly. 

But it doesn't stay that way. It's not this heavy, dark thing that sits on my chest all day long. Mary wouldn't stand for it if it was! She’s always bustling about, keeping the house going. If she sees me staring out the window too long, she’ll come over with a cup of tea or ask me to help her sort the coupons from the Sunday paper. And I still enjoy things, doctor. I still like my morning coffee, I still like watching the game shows at seven o'clock—even if the questions aren't nearly as hard as they used to be when Bob Barker was on television. 

So, no, not depressed. Not really. When I hear Thomas humming out there on the porch, it doesn't make me feel sad or down in the dumps. Honestly, sometimes it’s almost... comforting, in a strange way. It just reminds me of the choir days. I might feel a little wistful, sure, but I’m not sitting here crying or feeling hopeless from morning till night. I just get on with things. That's what you do when you're eighty-four, you just keep putting one foot in front of the other.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is a prominent mood syndrome that would better explain the psychotic symptoms and help distinguish schizophrenia from delusional disorder or an organic psychosis.
doctor.question: Have you had a period of several days when you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep than usual?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: On those nights I may sleep only two or three hours, then get up before daylight feeling ready to work like I had a full rest.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about needing much less sleep than usual, which directly maps to the decreased sleep symptom.

patient.answer:
Energetic? Less sleep? Well, now, that is an interesting question, doctor. Because Mary was just fussing at me about this very thing not two weeks ago. Usually, you see, we have our routine. We watch the Wheel of Fortune, maybe catch the ten o'clock local news, and then it's off to bed. At my age, you usually cherish a good night's sleep in a warm bed, especially with the arthritis and all. 

But every now and then... I don't know what gets into me, but I'll have these spells. They might last three or four days, sometimes near on a whole week, where my body just decides it doesn't need the pillow at all. On those nights I may sleep only two or three hours, then get up before daylight feeling ready to work like I had a full rest. 

It is the strangest thing, doctor. I'll lay my head down at ten, and by one or maybe half-past one in the morning, my eyes will just pop wide open. Wide open! And I'm not tossing and turning or feeling groggy, either. I'll feel so full of vinegar I can't just lay there staring at the ceiling, so I have to get up and do something. I'll go down to the kitchen, being real quiet on the stairs so I don't wake Mary, and I'll start finding chores. 

Last time it happened, I took apart the toaster to clean out all the burnt crumbs from the bottom, and then I got out my tools and oiled every single hinge on the kitchen cabinets. Mary came down at six in the morning in her pink robe, turned on the light, and just stared at me sitting there on the floor with a screwdriver. She said, "What on God's green earth are you doing up?" But I tried to tell her, I just didn't need the sleep! I felt fantastic. Back when I was working on the line at the plant, I would have paid good money to feel that spry for a morning shift. I could have worked a double shift and still had energy to mow the lawn. So yes, I do get those days where I just don't need much shut-eye at all and feel completely raring to go.

inference.note: New information suggests possible mania/hypomania features: episodes lasting 3–7 days with markedly decreased need for sleep and increased energy/activity. This adds F31.2 to prior psychotic-spectrum differentials. Primary delusional disorder remains plausible given late onset, relatively preserved cognition/function, and prominent persecutory/referential delusions; schizophrenia and organic psychosis still not excluded.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the reported decreased need for sleep and increased energy were accompanied by elevated or expansive mood, to distinguish mania with psychosis from primary psychotic or organic delusional disorders.

patient.answer: Cheerful? Oh, doctor, cheerful hardly does it justice. I feel... well, I wake up feeling just incredibly bright, you know? Like the sun is shining just for me and I'm the man of the hour. I'll feel so important, like I've got all the answers to everything. During those weeks—and it can go on for weeks sometimes, mind you

Primary psychotic disorders (F20.0, F22) and organic delusional disorder (F06.2) remain in the differential until full exclusion of medical/substance causes and longitudinal course are clarified.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated-energy, decreased-sleep spells include grandiosity severe enough to indicate mania, which would best distinguish bipolar disorder with psychotic features from primary psychotic disorders or psychosis due to a medical condition.
doctor.question: During those spells, did you feel you had special powers or abilities that other people did not have?

target_item.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
target_item.manifestation: I get sure that I am the one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again, like I have a special gift for making people listen and follow my plans.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about feeling like having special powers or abilities directly inquires about grandiosity or inflated self-esteem.

patient.answer:
Well, powers... I don't know if I'd call it magic powers, like you read about in comic books or see in those superhero movies the grandkids watch. But I do get this... this absolute certainty, doctor. It's like a fire in my belly. I get so sure that I am the one, the only one, who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. 

You see, our street used to be so close-knit back in the seventies. We had block parties, we all knew each other's dogs' names, we'd share tomatoes over the fence. Now, everyone just pulls into their garages and the doors go down. But during those spells, when I'm feeling so bright and full of energy, I just know I have a special gift for it. A real gift for making people listen and follow my plans. I'll sit at the kitchen table at two in the morning, drawing up these grand blueprints for community gardens and neighborhood watch schedules, and I just know that if I knock on their doors, they're all going to look at me and say, "Yes, absolutely, you're the man to lead us!" 

I feel like I have this incredible influence, this charm that just radiates out of me. I'll tell Mary, "Mary, I'm going to get the Miller boy to paint his fence, and I'm going to get the widow Jenkins to host a potluck, just you watch!" And I really believe it, doctor. I feel like I could walk out onto the porch and give a speech that would make the whole block fall in line, just because I have this... this special knack for it that nobody else around here has. It's a powerful feeling, let me tell you, knowing you're the one who holds the key to fixing how disconnected everyone's gotten. I just feel so capable, like I'm the mayor of the whole street and everyone is just waiting for my instructions.

inference.note: New evidence of decreased need for sleep, elevated mood, and grandiosity during spells strengthens F31.2. However, late-life onset with psychotic symptoms still leaves F20.0, F22, and F06.2 in the differential.
